title: Box Thirding: Anytime Best Arm Identification under Insufficient Sampling
topic: General Machine Learning->Online Learning, Active Learning and Bandits
claim: A hierarchical median-of-medians over small blocks yields a cheap, consistent estimate of the population median.
layout: 2 groups, left-to-right, three stacked rows feeding one result row via a big arrow
description: A toy numeric example in two parts. On the left, three stacked rows each contain three numbers in boxed cells: (1.0, 3.7, 2.8), (11.0, 5.3, 1.8) and (0.1, 8.2, 4.8). The median of each row is shaded light gray (2.8, 5.3, 4.8). A large blue block arrow points right to a single row of three cells holding those medians (2.8, 5.3, 4.8). In that row, the final median, 4.8, is shaded a darker gray. The figure uses black outlines on white with gray shading, so the eye goes to the blue arrow and then the dark-gray result. It shows blockwise medians feeding a median of medians, with no other labels or text.
caption: Toy example of remedian estimation: partition the data into three blocks and take their withinblock medians (2.8, 5.3, 4.8); taking the median of these medians yields 4.8. Repeating this hierarchical “median-of-medians” construction produces an estimator that converges in probability to the population
abstract: We introduce Box Thirding (B3), a flexible and efficient algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) under fixed-budget constraints. It is designed for both anytime BAI and scenarios with large N, where the number of arms is too large for exhaustive evaluation within a limited budget T. The algorithm employs an iterative ternary comparison: in each iteration, three arms are compared--the best-performing arm is explored further, the median is deferred for future comparisons, and the weakest is discarded. Even without prior knowledge of T, B3 achieves an epsilon-best arm misidentification probability comparable to Successive Halving (SH), which requires T as a predefined parameter, applied to a randomly selected subset of c0 arms that fit within the budget. Empirical results show that B3 outperforms existing methods under limited-budget constraints in terms of simple regret, as demonstrated on the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest dataset.
